stem: A 48-year-old man with depression that did not respond to two other drugs started a new antidepressant 3 weeks ago. At a dinner he eats aged cheese and cured meats and drinks red wine. Within 2 hours he develops a sudden pounding occipital headache, sweating and palpitations. Blood pressure is 230/145 mm Hg and heart rate is 118/min. He has no fever, no clonus and no diarrhea.
oneliner: 48M + refractory depression, new antidepressant + aged cheese and red wine + severe headache, sweating + BP 230/145 → which drug?
ask: Which of the following drugs is he most likely taking?

whyNot.B: **TCA**: anticholinergic effects and cardiac conduction toxicity; no tyramine crisis
whyNot.C: **SSRI**: risk is serotonin syndrome (fever, clonus, diarrhea), not food-triggered hypertension
whyNot.D: Lowers the **seizure threshold**; no tyramine interaction

why: **Severe headache + BP 230/145 after aged cheese and wine** = tyramine hypertensive crisis. **MAO inhibitors** such as tranylcypromine cannot break down tyramine, so it **displaces stored norepinephrine**.

drug.name: Tranylcypromine
drug.how: Irreversibly blocks MAO-A and MAO-B, raising norepinephrine, serotonin and dopamine
drug.use: Atypical or treatment-resistant depression, panic, phobias
drug.watch: Hypertensive crisis with tyramine foods, serotonin syndrome with SSRIs or meperidine, 2-week washout

stem: A 36-year-old man started fluoxetine for depression 2 weeks ago. Yesterday he began taking an over-the-counter amino acid supplement for sleep. Overnight he develops agitation, sweating, tremor and watery diarrhea. Temperature is 38.9 C, pupils are dilated, and he has hyperreflexia with inducible ankle clonus. Muscle tone is normal at rest.
oneliner: 36M + fluoxetine for 2 wk + new sleep supplement + agitation, diarrhea, fever + hyperreflexia, clonus → which supplement?
ask: Which of the following supplements most likely contributed to his condition?

whyNot.A: Made **from** tryptophan, but causes **flushing**, not serotonin excess
whyNot.B: Precursor of **SAM**, a methyl donor; not a serotonin precursor
whyNot.E: Inhibitory **spinal cord** transmitter; not a serotonin precursor

answer: Tryptophan (serotonin precursor) added to an SSRI
why: **SSRI + new supplement + hyperthermia, diarrhea, hyperreflexia and clonus** = serotonin syndrome. **Tryptophan** is the precursor of **serotonin**, so it adds to the serotonin already raised by fluoxetine.

drug.name: Tryptophan
drug.how: Converted to 5-hydroxytryptophan and then serotonin; adds to SSRI-raised serotonin
drug.use: Dietary protein; sold as a sleep or mood supplement
drug.watch: Serotonin syndrome with SSRIs or MAO inhibitors; eosinophilia-myalgia from contaminated supplements

stem: A 52-year-old woman with depression starts a new antidepressant. One week later she has dry mouth, blurred vision, constipation and difficulty emptying her bladder. Her pulse is 98/min. She is not dizzy on standing and has no sexual complaints.
oneliner: 52F + new antidepressant 1 wk + dry mouth, blurred vision, constipation, urinary retention → which receptor is blocked?
ask: Blockade of which of the following receptors best explains her constipation and urinary retention?

whyNot.A: Gives **sedation and weight gain**, not bladder or bowel slowing
whyNot.B: Gives **orthostatic hypotension**; she is not dizzy on standing
whyNot.C: Gives sedation and appetite change; **no anticholinergic picture**
whyNot.E: Gives **parkinsonism and prolactin rise**, not constipation and retention

why: **Dry mouth + blurred vision + constipation + urinary retention + tachycardia** = anticholinergic effects. **Tricyclic antidepressants** block **muscarinic receptors**.

drug.name: Amitriptyline
drug.how: Blocks norepinephrine and serotonin reuptake; also blocks muscarinic, H1 and alpha-1 receptors
drug.use: Depression, neuropathic pain, migraine prevention, insomnia
drug.watch: Anticholinergic effects, sedation, orthostasis, QRS widening and arrhythmia in overdose

stem: A 78-year-old man with diabetes has burning foot pain, and a drug taken at bedtime for the pain and poor sleep was started 2 weeks ago. He now has trouble starting his urine stream, dry mouth, constipation and new evening confusion. Pulse is 102/min. Bladder ultrasound shows a postvoid residual of 400 mL.
oneliner: 78M + diabetic foot pain, bedtime drug 2 wk + weak stream, dry mouth, constipation, confusion + PVR 400 mL → which drug?
ask: Which of the following drugs is most likely responsible?

whyNot.B: Gives **insomnia, tremor and seizures**; not anticholinergic
whyNot.C: Gives **hyponatremia, rash and bone marrow suppression**; weak anticholinergic effect
whyNot.D: SSRI: **GI upset, insomnia, sexual dysfunction**; little anticholinergic effect
whyNot.E: Gives **sedation, orthostasis and priapism**; little anticholinergic effect

why: **Dry mouth + constipation + urinary retention + confusion + tachycardia** is an anticholinergic picture in an older man. **Amitriptyline** is a **tricyclic with strong antimuscarinic action** used for neuropathic pain.

drug.name: Amitriptyline
drug.how: Blocks norepinephrine and serotonin reuptake; strong muscarinic, H1 and alpha-1 blockade
drug.use: Depression, neuropathic pain, migraine prevention, insomnia
drug.watch: Urinary retention, constipation, confusion in older adults, orthostasis, arrhythmia in overdose

stem: A 27-year-old man with schizophrenia had his haloperidol dose increased 4 days ago. He is now confused and diaphoretic with a temperature of 41 C, heart rate 124/min and blood pressure that swings between 90/60 and 170/105 mm Hg. He has severe generalized rigidity, reflexes are normal, and creatine kinase is 1,500 U/L. He has had no anesthesia, no new serotonergic drugs and no diarrhea.
oneliner: 27M + schizophrenia, haloperidol dose raised 4 d + fever 41 C, diaphoresis, labile BP + diffuse rigidity, normal reflexes + CK 1,500 → which problem?
ask: Which of the following is the most likely cause of his condition?

whyNot.A: Triggered by **volatile anesthetics or succinylcholine**; no anesthesia here
whyNot.B: Has **hyperreflexia, clonus and diarrhea**; none present
whyNot.C: Focal muscle spasm in the first days, but **no fever or high CK**
whyNot.D: Involuntary orofacial movements after **months to years**, not rigidity with fever

why: **Antipsychotic dose rise + fever + lead-pipe rigidity + autonomic instability + high CK** = neuroleptic malignant syndrome from **D2 blockade**. Stop the drug and give **dantrolene or bromocriptine**.

drug.name: Haloperidol
drug.watch: Extrapyramidal effects, neuroleptic malignant syndrome, tardive dyskinesia, QT prolongation, hyperprolactinemia

stem: A 34-year-old man was started on a new drug 6 days ago during his first psychiatric admission. He now moves slowly, has a masklike face and a shuffling gait with small steps, and has cogwheel rigidity in both arms. He has no fever, his sensorium is clear and there is no family history of movement disorder.
oneliner: 34M + new psychiatric drug 6 d + bradykinesia, masklike face, shuffling gait + cogwheel rigidity + no fever → which drug?
ask: Which of the following drugs most likely caused this?

whyNot.A: TCA: **anticholinergic and cardiac** effects; does not cause parkinsonism
whyNot.B: Benzodiazepine: **sedation and ataxia**, not rigidity and bradykinesia
whyNot.D: SSRI: GI upset and insomnia; **rarely** causes parkinsonism
whyNot.E: MAO inhibitor: **hypertensive crisis** and orthostasis, not parkinsonism

answer: Chlorpromazine (D2 blockade in the nigrostriatal pathway)
why: **Bradykinesia + cogwheel rigidity + shuffling gait within days of a psychotropic** = drug-induced parkinsonism. Antipsychotics such as **chlorpromazine** **block D2 receptors in the nigrostriatal pathway**.

drug.name: Chlorpromazine
drug.how: Blocks dopamine D2 receptors (also muscarinic, H1 and alpha-1)
drug.watch: Parkinsonism, sedation, anticholinergic effects, orthostasis, QT prolongation, corneal deposits

stem: A 22-year-old woman is brought in drowsy 35 minutes after swallowing an unknown number of her father's phenobarbital tablets. Respiratory rate is 6/min. Arterial blood gas on room air shows PaO2 53 mm Hg, PaCO2 70 mm Hg and an alveolar-arterial gradient of 9 mm Hg. Chest radiograph is clear, and she has not vomited.
oneliner: 22F + phenobarbital overdose 35 min ago + RR 6 + PaO2 53, PaCO2 70, A-a gradient 9 + clear chest film → what explains the hypoxemia?
ask: Which of the following best explains her hypoxemia?

whyNot.A: Raises the **A-a gradient**; hers is normal
whyNot.C: Raises the **A-a gradient** and does not correct with oxygen; **PaCO2 would not climb**
whyNot.D: Raises the **A-a gradient**; the chest film is clear
whyNot.E: Tested on **room air at sea level**; gradient would be normal but **PaCO2 would not rise**

why: **High PaCO2 + low PaO2 + normal A-a gradient** = pure hypoventilation. **Barbiturates** prolong **GABA-A chloride channel opening** and depress the **brainstem respiratory drive**.

drug.name: Phenobarbital
drug.how: Increases the duration of GABA-A chloride channel opening
drug.watch: Respiratory depression in overdose, CYP450 induction, dependence, cannot be reversed with flumazenil

stem: A 2-year-old girl is brought in 30 minutes after her mother found her with an open bottle of the mother's diazepam, with about 10 tablets missing. She is awake, playful and has normal vital signs. The physician plans prolonged observation.
oneliner: 2F + swallowed mother's diazepam ~10 tablets 30 min ago + currently awake, normal vitals → which complication is the main worry?
ask: Which of the following is the most serious complication to watch for?

whyNot.A: Seen in **benzodiazepine withdrawal** or with TCA or bupropion overdose, not benzodiazepine overdose

answer: Respiratory depression and CNS depression (benzodiazepine overdose)
why: **Benzodiazepine overdose** mainly causes **CNS and respiratory depression**, which can appear late in a child. Management is **supportive**; **flumazenil** is rarely used.

drug.name: Diazepam
drug.how: Enhances GABA-A chloride channel opening frequency
drug.use: Anxiety, status epilepticus, muscle spasm, alcohol withdrawal
drug.watch: Overdose: CNS and respiratory depression, worse with alcohol or opioids; flumazenil can precipitate seizures in chronic users

stem: A 31-year-old woman comes to the emergency department with abdominal cramps, vomiting, a runny nose, tearing, yawning and goose bumps. Her pupils are dilated and she has had loose stools. She is alert and oriented, not tremulous, and has no seizure history. Blood pressure is 142/90 mm Hg. Forearm examination shows several old track marks.
oneliner: 31F + cramps, vomiting, rhinorrhea, lacrimation, yawning, piloerection + dilated pupils + alert, no tremor + old track marks → which substance was stopped?
ask: Withdrawal from which of the following substances best explains her findings?

whyNot.A: Withdrawal gives **tremor, seizures and delirium**, not rhinorrhea and piloerection
whyNot.C: Withdrawal is a **crash**: fatigue, hypersomnia, depression, hunger
whyNot.D: Withdrawal is also a **crash** with fatigue and increased appetite
whyNot.E: Withdrawal gives **irritability, craving and increased appetite**

why: **Rhinorrhea + lacrimation + yawning + piloerection + dilated pupils + cramps** with track marks = opioid withdrawal: **miserable but not life threatening**. Treat with **methadone or buprenorphine**, or **clonidine** for symptoms.

drug.name: Heroin (opioids)
drug.how: Activates mu receptors; sedation, miosis, respiratory depression
drug.use: Illicit; related drugs treat pain, cough and diarrhea
drug.watch: Overdose: coma, miosis, respiratory depression (naloxone); withdrawal: rhinorrhea, piloerection, yawning, diarrhea, mydriasis

stem: A 24-year-old man collapsed at a party and could not be resuscitated. Friends say he had been using a drug that morning. Autopsy shows a structurally normal heart with patent coronary arteries, and toxicology is positive for cocaine.
oneliner: 24M + collapse and death at a party + normal heart, patent coronaries at autopsy + cocaine on toxicology → which mechanism caused the arrhythmia?
ask: Which of the following actions most likely led to his fatal arrhythmia?

options.E: Blocked reuptake of norepinephrine at sympathetic nerve terminals

whyNot.C: **Verapamil / diltiazem**: slows the heart and AV node

answer: Blocked norepinephrine reuptake, causing catecholamine excess and arrhythmia
why: **Sudden death + cocaine + normal heart** = catecholamine-driven arrhythmia. **Cocaine blocks presynaptic reuptake of norepinephrine, dopamine and serotonin**, so synaptic norepinephrine overstimulates **beta-1 receptors**.

drug.name: Cocaine
drug.how: Blocks reuptake of norepinephrine, dopamine and serotonin; also blocks sodium channels
drug.watch: Arrhythmia, MI, vasospasm, hypertension, aortic dissection, seizures, nasal septum perforation, mydriasis

stem: A 17-year-old boy is brought from a party after staring blankly with a rigid posture and then suddenly becoming violent toward bystanders. Pulse is 84/min and blood pressure is 128/78 mm Hg. Pupils are of normal size and he has vertical nystagmus. His speech is slurred and he does not respond to questions.
oneliner: 17M + party + blank stare, rigidity, sudden violence + normal HR and BP, normal pupils + vertical nystagmus → which substance?
ask: Which of the following substances most likely caused this presentation?

whyNot.A: Gives **dilated pupils** and chest pain; **no vertical nystagmus** or catatonic stare
whyNot.B: Gives **dilated pupils** and paranoia; **no vertical nystagmus**
whyNot.D: Gives **visual distortions and dilated pupils**; no nystagmus or catatonia
whyNot.E: Gives **miosis, sedation and slow breathing**; pupils here are normal

why: **Blank stare + rigidity + sudden violence + vertical nystagmus + normal vitals** = **phencyclidine** intoxication. It blocks the **NMDA receptor**. Watch for **rhabdomyolysis**.

drug.name: Phencyclidine (PCP)
drug.use: Illicit; ketamine is the related anesthetic
drug.watch: Violence, psychosis, vertical or horizontal nystagmus, rhabdomyolysis, hyperthermia, seizures

stem: A 26-year-old man took amphetamine tablets prescribed to his friend for attention deficit disorder to stay awake for an examination. He is now restless and irritable with a tremor and sweating. Pulse is 122/min, blood pressure is 168/98 mm Hg and pupils are dilated. His skin is moist and bowel sounds are normal.
oneliner: 26M + friend's amphetamine ADHD tablets + restless, irritable, tremor, sweaty + HR 122, BP 168/98 + dilated pupils, moist skin → which mechanism?
ask: Which of the following best explains his findings?

options.A: Blocked reuptake alone without release of stored amines
options.B: Increased release and decreased reuptake of catecholamines

whyNot.A: **Cocaine and methylphenidate** act this way; amphetamine also releases stored amines
whyNot.C: **Opioids** cause miosis, sedation and a slow pulse
whyNot.D: **Anticholinergics** cause dry skin and absent bowel sounds; his skin is moist
whyNot.E: **Cannabis** gives conjunctival injection and hunger with mild tachycardia

why: **ADHD tablets + tremor + sweating + tachycardia + hypertension + mydriasis** = sympathetic overstimulation. **Amphetamine releases and blocks reuptake of norepinephrine and dopamine**.

drug.name: Amphetamine
drug.how: Releases norepinephrine and dopamine and blocks their reuptake
drug.watch: Intoxication: agitation, tachycardia, hypertension, mydriasis, sweating, psychosis; urine acidification speeds elimination

stem: A 70-year-old woman started amitriptyline two weeks ago for depression with neuropathic pain. She has had two near-falls from dizziness on standing up. Blood pressure is 128/76 mm Hg lying down and 92/58 mm Hg standing, with a heart rate of 80/min lying and 96/min standing. She also feels drowsy during the day.
oneliner: 70F + amitriptyline for 2 weeks + dizziness on standing + BP 128/76 → 92/58 + drowsy → which receptor blockade explains the BP change?
ask: Blockade of which receptor best explains her fall in blood pressure on standing?

options.A: Muscarinic M3 receptor blockade in the bladder and gut
options.B: Histamine H1 receptor blockade in the brain
options.C: Alpha-1 adrenergic receptor blockade in the vessel wall
options.D: Beta-1 adrenergic receptor blockade in the sinus node and myocardium
options.E: Dopamine D2 receptor blockade in the nigrostriatal pathway

whyNot.A: Explains **dry mouth, constipation and urinary retention**, not a drop in blood pressure
whyNot.B: Explains her **daytime drowsiness**, not the **orthostatic fall in pressure**
whyNot.D: Would **blunt the heart rate rise** on standing; her pulse rose appropriately
whyNot.E: Causes **parkinsonism**, not an **orthostatic fall in pressure**; tricyclics have little D2 effect

why: **Tricyclics** block **alpha-1 receptors**, so vessels cannot constrict on standing and she has **orthostatic hypotension** with falls. Their **H1** blockade causes **sedation**, and **M3** blockade causes anticholinergic effects.

drug.name: Amitriptyline
drug.how: Blocks serotonin and norepinephrine reuptake; also blocks muscarinic, H1 and alpha-1 receptors
drug.use: Depression, neuropathic pain, migraine prophylaxis, insomnia
drug.watch: Orthostatic hypotension (alpha-1), sedation (H1), anticholinergic effects, QRS widening and seizures in overdose

idea.rule: Tricyclic side effects map to the receptors they block: M3, H1 and alpha-1.
also: M3 blockade: dry mouth, constipation, urinary retention
H1 blockade: sedation and weight gain
Alpha-1 blockade: orthostatic hypotension
Sodium channel blockade: QRS widening in overdose (treat with bicarbonate)

stem: A 29-year-old man started on sertraline 6 weeks ago for depression. His mood has improved, but he now has little interest in sex and takes a long time to reach orgasm. He is alert during the day, has no dry mouth or urinary hesitancy, and does not become lightheaded on standing.
oneliner: 29M + sertraline for depression + low libido, delayed orgasm + alert by day + no dry mouth, no urinary hesitancy, no orthostasis → which adverse effect?
ask: These symptoms are best explained by which adverse effect of the drug?

whyNot.A: Needs **antimuscarinic** action; he has **no hesitancy or dry mouth**
whyNot.B: Comes from **alpha-1 blockade**; he has **no lightheadedness on standing**
whyNot.C: Typical of **mirtazapine or trazodone** (H1 blockade); he is **alert during the day**
whyNot.E: Typical of **trazodone** (alpha-blockade); his problem is **reduced** sexual function

why: SSRIs raise synaptic serotonin, and this commonly causes **delayed orgasm and low libido** (sexual dysfunction), plus GI upset. SSRIs have **little antimuscarinic, antihistamine or alpha-blocking activity**, which is why dry mouth, retention, sedation and orthostasis are absent.

drug.name: Sertraline
drug.how: Blocks the serotonin transporter (SERT), raising synaptic serotonin
drug.use: Depression, anxiety disorders, OCD, PTSD, panic disorder
drug.watch: Sexual dysfunction, GI upset, insomnia, serotonin syndrome with MAOIs, hyponatremia (SIADH), bleeding risk

idea.rule: SSRIs are clean of antimuscarinic effects; their signature problem is sexual dysfunction.
also: Bupropion and mirtazapine cause less sexual dysfunction
TCAs: dry mouth, retention, constipation
Trazodone: sedation, priapism
Paroxetine is the most antimuscarinic SSRI

stem: A 22-year-old woman with bulimia nervosa begins a new medication to help her stop smoking. Three days later she has a generalized tonic-clonic seizure. She has no history of epilepsy, and she has had no sexual side effects or weight gain from the drug.
oneliner: 22F + bulimia nervosa + new smoking-cessation antidepressant + generalized seizure on day 3 + no sexual side effects or weight gain → which drug?
ask: Which drug most likely caused the seizure?

whyNot.A: An SSRI; it is **not a smoking-cessation drug**, and it commonly causes **sexual side effects**
whyNot.C: Used for **insomnia** and causes **priapism and sedation**, not smoking cessation
whyNot.D: Causes **weight gain and sedation**, which she has not had
whyNot.E: An SNRI; it is **not a smoking-cessation drug**, and it commonly causes **sexual side effects**

why: **Bupropion** is an antidepressant used for **smoking cessation**, and it **lowers the seizure threshold**. It is avoided in **seizure disorders and in bulimia or anorexia** because purging and low weight add to the risk.

drug.name: Bupropion
drug.how: Inhibits reuptake of norepinephrine and dopamine
drug.use: Depression, smoking cessation, seasonal affective disorder
drug.watch: Seizures (contraindicated in bulimia, anorexia, seizure disorders), insomnia, dry mouth, headache; no sexual dysfunction or weight gain

idea.rule: Bupropion: smoking cessation, no sexual side effects, but seizure risk.
also: Contraindicated in bulimia and anorexia nervosa
Weight-neutral or weight-loss antidepressant
Varenicline is the other main smoking-cessation drug
Avoid during abrupt alcohol or benzodiazepine withdrawal

stem: A 50-year-old man takes an antidepressant each night to help him sleep. He wakes at 4 AM with a painful erection that has lasted 5 hours and does not settle. He says the medication makes him drowsy, and he has no dry mouth or constipation.
oneliner: 50M + nightly antidepressant for insomnia + drowsy + no dry mouth or constipation + painful erection 5 hours → which drug?
ask: Which drug most likely caused the finding?

whyNot.A: **Activating**, not a sleep aid; he is **drowsy** on his drug, and priapism is not its effect
whyNot.B: Usually **activating** and taken in the morning; he is **drowsy**, and priapism is not its hallmark
whyNot.C: Sedating, but **antimuscarinic**; he has **no dry mouth or constipation**, and priapism is not its hallmark
whyNot.D: An SNRI that is **activating** (insomnia), not a bedtime sedative; priapism is not its effect

why: **Trazodone** is sedating (H1 and 5-HT2A blockade), so low doses are used at bedtime. Its **alpha-1 blockade** can cause **priapism** and orthostasis, and it has little antimuscarinic action.

drug.name: Trazodone
drug.class: Atypical antidepressant (serotonin antagonist and reuptake inhibitor)
drug.how: Blocks 5-HT2A and H1 receptors and weakly inhibits serotonin reuptake; alpha-1 blockade

also: Low-dose trazodone is a common hypnotic
Alpha-1 blockade also causes orthostatic hypotension
Treat priapism with intracavernosal phenylephrine
Prazosin and chlorpromazine can also cause priapism

stem: A 40-year-old woman who has taken alprazolam daily for 3 years is brought in after a deliberate overdose, drowsy but breathing, with oxygen saturation 97%. Glucose and sodium are normal. She is given an intravenous antidote that reverses the sedative, and minutes later she has a generalized tonic-clonic seizure.
oneliner: 40F + daily alprazolam for 3 years + intentional overdose + SpO2 97%, normal glucose and sodium + IV antidote → seizure minutes later → why?

options.B: Hypoxic brain injury from the overdose

whyNot.B: She was **breathing with saturation 97%**, so there was no hypoxia
whyNot.D: Benzodiazepines are **anticonvulsants**; the seizure came **minutes after the antidote**

why: The antidote is **flumazenil**, a **benzodiazepine-site antagonist** at the GABA-A receptor. In a **chronic daily user** it abruptly removes GABA tone and **precipitates withdrawal seizures**. Overdose alone mainly causes sedation and respiratory depression.

drug.name: Flumazenil
drug.how: Competitively blocks the benzodiazepine site on the GABA-A receptor
drug.use: Reversal of benzodiazepine sedation or overdose
drug.watch: Seizures in dependent patients or mixed overdose (especially with TCAs), short half-life so resedation can recur

idea.rule: Flumazenil can precipitate seizures in a benzodiazepine-dependent patient.
also: Naloxone in opioid-dependent patients precipitates withdrawal
Avoid flumazenil with co-ingested TCAs or seizure history
Supportive airway care is the usual treatment for benzodiazepine overdose
Benzodiazepine withdrawal itself can cause seizures

stem: A 28-year-old man with schizophrenia that did not respond to two other antipsychotics has been on a newer drug for 10 weeks. He now has fever and a sore throat. The white cell count is 2,100/µL with an absolute neutrophil count of 150/µL.
oneliner: 28M + schizophrenia resistant to two antipsychotics + 10 weeks of new drug + fever, sore throat + ANC 150 → which drug?
ask: Which drug most likely caused these findings?

whyNot.A: A high-potency typical agent; its hallmark is **extrapyramidal symptoms**, and it is not reserved for **resistant** disease
whyNot.B: Raises **prolactin**; not reserved for **resistant** disease, and agranulocytosis is not its hallmark
whyNot.C: Causes **weight gain and metabolic syndrome**; not reserved for **resistant** disease
whyNot.E: A partial D2 agonist with **akathisia**; not reserved for **resistant** disease or linked to agranulocytosis

why: **Clozapine** is kept for **treatment-resistant schizophrenia** and can cause **agranulocytosis**, so the **absolute neutrophil count** is monitored. It also **lowers the seizure threshold** and causes myocarditis and sialorrhea.

drug.name: Clozapine
drug.how: Antagonizes D2 weakly and 5-HT2A, with strong muscarinic, H1 and alpha-1 effects
drug.watch: Agranulocytosis (monitor ANC), seizures, myocarditis, sialorrhea, weight gain and metabolic syndrome

idea.rule: Clozapine is reserved for resistant schizophrenia and needs neutrophil monitoring.
also: Also lowers the seizure threshold
Myocarditis and hypersalivation
Carbamazepine also causes agranulocytosis and aplastic anemia
Lowest risk of extrapyramidal symptoms among antipsychotics

stem: A 41-year-old man taking phenelzine for depression is given meperidine for postoperative pain. Hours later he is febrile and agitated, with diarrhea and sweating. Examination shows hyperreflexia and inducible ankle clonus in both legs.
oneliner: 41M + phenelzine + new meperidine + fever, agitation + diarrhea, diaphoresis + hyperreflexia and inducible clonus → complication?
ask: Which of the following complications is most likely?

whyNot.A: NMS follows **dopamine blockers** and brings **lead-pipe rigidity with decreased reflexes**, not clonus
whyNot.B: Tyramine crisis gives **severe headache and hypertension** after food, not diarrhea and clonus
whyNot.C: Anticholinergic toxicity gives **dry skin and dilated pupils**; he is sweating with diarrhea
whyNot.E: Malignant hyperthermia follows **anesthetic gases or succinylcholine** with rigidity, not clonus

why: An **MAO inhibitor plus a serotonergic drug (meperidine)** causes **serotonin syndrome**: **hyperthermia, agitation, clonus, hyperreflexia, diarrhea**. Treat by stopping the drugs; **cyproheptadine** helps, and MAOIs need a **2-week washout** before switching.

drug.name: Phenelzine
drug.how: Irreversibly inhibits monoamine oxidase, raising serotonin, norepinephrine and dopamine
drug.use: Atypical depression and phobic anxiety after other agents fail
drug.watch: Serotonin syndrome with meperidine, SSRIs or dextromethorphan (2-week washout), hypertensive crisis with tyramine foods, orthostasis, weight gain

idea.rule: MAOI plus a serotonergic drug = serotonin syndrome (clonus, hyperreflexia, diarrhea, fever).
also: SSRIs
Meperidine
Dextromethorphan
Linezolid
Tryptophan supplements
